items.followUp: State one limitation of Newlands’ law of octaves.

rubric.why: The elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic mass.
rubric.description: States the basis for arranging the elements.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that elements are arranged by increasing atomic mass.

rubric.why: The defining observation is that every eighth element has properties similar to the first.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that every eighth element has properties similar to the first.

modelAnswer: Newlands arranged the elements in order of increasing atomic masses.
He observed that the properties of every eighth element were similar to those of the first, like notes in an octave.

items.followUp: Explain why atomic size decreases from left to right across a period.

rubric.why: An additional electron shell is added at each step down a group.
rubric.description: Identifies the addition of electron shells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the number of electron shells increases down a group.

rubric.why: The added shells place the outermost electrons farther from the nucleus, increasing atomic size.
rubric.description: Links added shells to greater atomic size.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the outermost electrons are farther from the nucleus.

modelAnswer: Moving down a group, each successive element has an additional electron shell.
The outermost electrons are therefore farther from the nucleus, so atomic size increases.

items.followUp: Where are transition metals located in the periodic table?

rubric.why: Transition metals are characterized by partially filled d orbitals.
rubric.description: Identifies the partially filled d subshell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for mentioning partially filled or incomplete d orbitals.

rubric.why: The d subshell may be partially filled in the atom or in one of its ions.
rubric.description: Specifies where the d subshell is partially filled.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that this occurs in their atoms or ions.

modelAnswer: Transition metals are elements that have partially filled d orbitals in their atoms or in one of their ions.

items.followUp: Give two common uses of metals based on their properties.

rubric.why: Conductivity is a major property of metals.
rubric.description: Gives a conductivity property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals conduct heat or electricity.

rubric.why: Malleability, ductility, and lustre are common properties of metals.
rubric.description: Gives another major property of metals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that metals are malleable, ductile, or lustrous.

modelAnswer: Metals are good conductors of heat and electricity.
Metals are malleable and can be beaten into sheets.

items.followUp: Give two differences between ionic and covalent compounds.

rubric.why: Polar compounds have unequal charge distribution, whereas non-polar compounds have an even distribution.
rubric.description: Contrasts charge distribution in polar and non-polar compounds.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting unequal and equal charge distribution or sharing.

rubric.why: Polar compounds have a net dipole moment; non-polar compounds have none.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly contrasting the presence and absence of a net dipole moment.

modelAnswer: In a polar compound, charge is distributed unequally; in a non-polar compound, charge is distributed evenly.
A polar compound has a net dipole moment, whereas a non-polar compound has no net dipole moment.

rubric.description: Identifies boiling point as a temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it is a temperature.

rubric.why: Boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid boils and changes to gas; equivalently, its vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Describes the boiling change or its pressure condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the liquid changes into gas at this temperature, or that its vapour pressure equals atmospheric pressure.

modelAnswer: The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas throughout the liquid.

items.followUp: What is meant by a solute? Give one example.

rubric.why: A solvent is the substance that dissolves the solute.
rubric.description: States the solvent’s role in a solution.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solvent dissolves another substance.

rubric.why: Water, ethanol, and benzene are examples of solvents.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of a solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a suitable solvent.

modelAnswer: A solvent is the substance in which a solute dissolves to form a solution.
Water is an example of a solvent.

items.followUp: What is the solubility of a substance at a particular temperature?

rubric.why: Solubility refers to the maximum amount of solute that dissolves.
rubric.description: Identifies the maximum amount of solute.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that solubility is the maximum amount or quantity of solute that dissolves.

rubric.why: The textbook definition specifies the amount that dissolves in 100 g of solvent to form a saturated solution at a given temperature.
rubric.description: Includes the solvent mass, saturated solution, and temperature condition.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for specifying 100 g of solvent and formation of a saturated solution at a particular temperature.

modelAnswer: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that dissolves in 100 g of a solvent to form a saturated solution at a particular temperature.
